# 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow Disasters

## The De Havilland Vampire Crash: Vortex-Induced Loss of Control

The first of the two catastrophic incidents that defined the 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow occurred on Saturday, June 2, 2001 . At approximately 6:00 PM BST (17:10 UTC), a restored De Havilland D.H. 115 Vampire T.11 trainer jet spiraled out of control and crashed during its final display sequence of the day , . The aircraft, registered as G-AMRB and formerly operated by the Swiss Air Force, was participating in a formation flight with a larger lead aircraft, identified in several sources as a DH Sea Vixen , , . The disaster unfolded near Bromley in Kent, about 1.5 miles from London Biggin Hill Airport, when the smaller Vampire encountered powerful aerodynamic forces generated by the larger jet , . Specifically, the Vampire became uncontrollable after being sucked into a powerful air vortex and experiencing strong jet efflux from the Sea Vixen as it banked sharply in front of it , . This encounter caused the Vampire to roll inverted, enter an uncontrolled dive at a steep angle while banking heavily to the right, and plummet towards the ground . The aircraft corkscrewed twice before impacting a ridge and disintegrating in a massive fireball, an explosion described as being "louder than thunder" , . The entire sequence from loss of control to impact lasted approximately five seconds . No injuries were reported among the estimated 35,000 spectators who witnessed the event .

The aircraft was carrying two individuals whose identities would later underscore the profound tragedy of the event. The pilot was Sir Kenneth Hayr, a 66-year-old retired Royal Air Force (RAF) Air Marshal and former Deputy Chief of Defence Staff , , . Sir Ken Hayr had a distinguished military career, serving in both the Falklands and Gulf Wars, and was notably responsible for planning the RAF's role in Operation Desert Storm . He was decorated with the Order of the British Empire (KBE) and the Kuwait Liberation Order (first grade) in recognition of his service . His presence in the cockpit transformed the incident from a routine aviation mishap into a significant national event, symbolizing the vulnerability even of the most senior figures in the UK's defense establishment. The co-pilot was Jonathan Kerr, also known as Jim Kerr, a 32- or 33-year-old electronics engineer from Bournemouth , , . Kerr's background represented the passion and dedication of the vintage aviation restoration community; he was widely reported to have reassembled and flown the Vampire himself , . The combination of a top-tier military commander and a dedicated amateur enthusiast highlighted the diverse spectrum of individuals drawn to the art of aerial display flying. Both men died instantly upon impact . The Croydon Coroner's Court later returned a formal verdict of accidental death for both pilots following an inquest , . The families of the deceased jointly cremated the pilots' remains and scattered their ashes at Biggin Hill in a poignant tribute . The MoD and the RAF issued formal condolences, acknowledging the loss of two prominent figures from the nation's aviation community .

## The Bell P-63 Kingcobra Crash: A Pilot-Induced Aerodynamic Failure

Less than 24 hours after the tragic loss of Sir Kenneth Hayr and Jonathan Kerr, the Biggin Hill Airshow was plunged into a second catastrophe on Sunday, June 3, 2001 , . During the American fighter demonstration sequence, approximately five minutes into the display, a Bell P-63A Kingcobra fighter, registered as G-BTWR and operated by The Fighter Collection at Duxford, met a similar fate , . The aircraft entered an upright incipient spin at the top of a vertical loop maneuver while flying partially inverted , . Despite an attempt to recover from the developing spin, the pilot was unable to regain control, and the aircraft failed to recover, crashing into the ground in a steep nose-down attitude at a speed of approximately 160 knots , . The impact resulted in the complete destruction of the airframe and triggered an immediate post-impact fire, creating another large explosion and fireball in front of the 50,000 spectators present , . Eyewitnesses described the crash as occurring just 100 yards from where they were standing . Following this second fatal accident, the airfield was immediately closed and the remainder of the airshow was suspended entirely, bringing the disastrous weekend to a close , . It is important to note that one source contained a significant factual error, mistakenly identifying Richard Green, a witness filming the crash, as the pilot . The correct identity of the pilot is Guy Bancroft-Wilson , .

The investigation into the Kingcobra crash, conducted by the UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB), concluded that the primary cause was the pilot's actions . The AAIB report determined that Guy Bancroft-Wilson entered the final aerial loop of his display with insufficient speed, a condition most likely resulting from a continuing loss of energy after a preceding maneuver . The detailed narrative of the flight sequence provided in the AAIB report illustrates the progression of the failure. After a flypast at 220 knots, the aircraft executed a rolling climbing manoeuvre, from which it recovered from an incipient spin, followed by a left wingover and a return pass at 190–195 knots , . The subsequent loop entry involved the application of full nose-up elevator and substantial right rudder, which led to yaw and the departure into a spin from which recovery was not possible . The AAIB report noted that it was "difficult to understand why the pilot, who was experienced and practised in the display environment, continued with his display" despite the evident lack of kinetic energy . This finding points towards a potential lapse in judgment or situational awareness rather than a mechanical failure of the aircraft itself. The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) subsequently cancelled the aircraft registration G-BTWR on August 28, 2002, as a direct consequence of the crash , . The crash of the Kingcobra, like that of the Vampire, was a stark reminder of the inherent risks of performing complex aerobatic maneuvers at low altitudes in front of a large audience.

## The Airshow Environment and Organizational Response

The 2001 edition of the Biggin Hill International Air Fair was in its 39th year and was attracting an expected crowd of around 35,000 people each day , . The event, held annually at the historic airfield near Bromley, Kent, is renowned for its displays of vintage and classic military aircraft. The atmosphere on the opening day, Saturday, June 2, was typical of such a gathering until the fateful crash of the De Havilland Vampire occurred . In the immediate aftermath of the Vampire crash, the organizers faced a crisis of unprecedented severity. The decision-making process was swift but fraught with complexity. Initially, the airshow proceeded on the following day, Sunday, June 3, after organizers consulted with members of the team associated with the deceased pilots, Sir Kenneth Hayr and Jonathan Kerr , . This decision to continue the event can be interpreted as a gesture of respect for the fallen pilots and their teams, a desire to honor their memory by completing the scheduled program, and a pragmatic assessment of the situation at the time. However, this choice created a psychologically charged environment for the remaining performers and attendees, a somber backdrop against which the second tragedy unfolded less than 24 hours later. The decision to suspend the remainder of the airshow on Monday, June 4, following the crash of the Bell P-63 Kingcobra, demonstrated a belated but decisive shift in priorities, moving from maintaining the schedule to unequivocally prioritizing safety over all other considerations , , .

The organizational response to the dual disasters included an immediate launch of official investigations. On the evening of the second crash, Chief Superintendent Gerry Howlett of Kent Police addressed the media at a press conference, confirming the preliminary findings that the Kingcobra had entered a vertical maneuver near the display center, failed to recover, and crashed northwest of the runway . He also stated that the Kingcobra had exploded in a fireball nose-first into the ground in front of the spectators . The UK Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) launched a formal inquiry into both crashes, tasked with determining the precise technical and procedural causes , , . The seriousness of the situation prompted an acknowledgment from Air Displays International, the event's organizers, who admitted the likelihood of a formal review of safety procedures in the wake of the tragedies . The term "disasters," used in the user's query and echoed in contemporary discussions, aptly captures the gravity of the event, which was described by one eyewitness forum contributor as "probably the worst weekend in modern airshow history in the UK" . The clustering of two fatal accidents within such a short period fundamentally altered the airshow's reputation and trajectory. While the event has historically been considered safe, having no prior fatalities since 1980, the 2001 incidents shattered that perception and forced a critical reassessment of risk management in live aerial demonstrations , . The rapid suspension of the show served as a clear signal to the industry and the public that the stakes were higher than ever, and that the line between thrilling entertainment and deadly hazard had been dangerously crossed.

## Victim Profiles and Public Reaction

The personal stories of the pilots killed in the 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters lent immense weight and emotional resonance to the tragedies, transforming them from mere statistical occurrences into deeply human stories of loss. The profiles of the three deceased men—Sir Kenneth Hayr, Jonathan Kerr, and Guy Bancroft-Wilson—spanned the entire spectrum of experience in aviation, from the highest echelons of military command to the passionate world of private restoration and elite professional display flying. This diversity underscored a crucial lesson from the disasters: that the unique hazards of airshows pose a threat to all participants, regardless of skill, rank, or experience. Sir Kenneth Hayr's death was particularly significant due to his prominent public profile. As a retired RAF Air Marshal and former Deputy Chief of Defence Staff, he was a respected figure within the UK's defense community and a veteran of major conflicts , . His involvement in planning the RAF's strategic role in the Gulf War made him a key architect of modern air power doctrine . His presence in the cockpit of a vintage Vampire was a testament to his lifelong passion for flying, but his death was a profound blow to the military establishment and a symbolic loss for the nation's commemoration of its defense heritage . His wife, Joyce, had passed away in 1987, leaving behind three sons .

In contrast to Sir Ken Hayr's professional military career, Jonathan Kerr embodied the spirit of the dedicated aviation enthusiast. Described as an electronics engineer from Bournemouth who had personally reassembled the Vampire he flew, Kerr represented the thousands of volunteers and hobbyists who keep the history of aviation alive through restoration projects , . His story was one of pure passion, driven by a love for the machines and the challenge of returning them to the skies. His death was a devastating loss for his family and the wider vintage aircraft community . The third victim, Guy Bancroft-Wilson, presented a more complex case. A 43-year-old British Airways captain based at Gatwick Airport, he was also a former RAF officer and a member of the famed Red Arrows aerobatic team . His credentials placed him among the elite of professional aviators. His death was therefore particularly sobering, challenging the assumption that extensive experience in one domain, such as commercial airline operations, necessarily guarantees infallibility in the vastly different and more demanding environment of aerobatic displays. The AAIB's puzzlement over his decision to continue his display despite entering a maneuver with insufficient speed raised questions about situational awareness and decision-making under pressure, even for highly skilled pilots . The public reaction to these deaths was one of shock and grief, amplified by the high-profile nature of the victims and the graphic nature of the crashes witnessed live by tens of thousands of people. The images of fireballs erupting in the sky over the airfield left a lasting impression, fundamentally altering public perception of the event's safety and marking the 2001 airshow as a dark chapter in its otherwise long history.

## Investigations, Verdicts, and Official Findings

Following the twin tragedies of the 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow, two distinct but equally important official processes were initiated to determine the causes of the crashes and provide closure to the families of the deceased. The first process was a criminal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the deaths, culminating in a coroner's inquest. The second was a technical and procedural investigation conducted by the UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB), which focused on the operational and mechanical factors that led to the accidents. The findings from both bodies were crucial in understanding the different modes of failure that occurred and in shaping future safety recommendations for airshow operations. The inquest into the death of the two pilots from the De Havilland Vampire crash opened on May 14, 2002, in Croydon, Surrey . Testimony heard during the proceedings confirmed that the aircraft became uncontrollable after encountering wingtip vortices and jet efflux from a lead DH Sea Vixen aircraft during a formation flight , . The jury at the inquest returned a verdict of accidental death for both Sir Kenneth Hayr and Jonathan Kerr, formally concluding that the crashes were unintentional events caused by unforeseen aerodynamic forces , . This verdict absolved the pilots of any fault in initiating the maneuvers but pointed squarely to the environmental conditions and the dynamics of formation flying as the root cause of the accident.

The investigation into the Bell P-63 Kingcobra crash was handled exclusively by the AAIB, which published a detailed accident investigation report . The AAIB's analysis focused on the specific flight sequence leading up to the crash, reconstructing the pilot's actions with precision. According to the report, the crash was directly attributable to pilot-induced aerodynamic failure . The investigation established that the pilot, Guy Bancroft-Wilson, had entered the final loop maneuver with 'insufficient speed', a condition likely exacerbated by a continuing loss of energy from a preceding maneuver . The application of full nose-up elevator and substantial right rudder during the loop initiation caused the aircraft to depart into an upright incipient spin from which recovery was impossible , . The AAIB report expressed a degree of uncertainty regarding the pilot's decision-making, noting it was "difficult to understand why the pilot... continued with his display" given the state of his aircraft . This finding suggests that while the immediate physical cause was the spin, the underlying cause may have been a lapse in judgment or a misjudgment of the aircraft's energy state. The report meticulously documented the speeds at various points in the maneuver, providing a clear timeline of how the aircraft lost control , . The combined findings from the coroner's court and the AAIB paint a clear picture of two distinct failures: one caused by external, unpredictable aerodynamic forces beyond the pilots' control, and the other stemming from internal factors related to the pilot's decisions and the aircraft's performance envelope. These comprehensive investigations were essential for preventing similar incidents in the future and for providing a factual basis for the ongoing dialogue about safety in the world of airshow displays.

## Legacy and Historical Context

The 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters represent a pivotal moment in the history of the event and the broader context of public aviation displays in the United Kingdom. The legacy of the twin crashes is multifaceted, encompassing changes in safety protocols, a permanent alteration in public perception, and a renewed focus on the inherent risks of vintage airshow flying. The immediate and dramatic suspension of the airshow following the second crash served as a stark warning to the organizers and the entire industry , . While the specific long-term regulatory changes implemented *directly* as a result of these two incidents are not detailed in the provided sources, it is highly probable that they contributed significantly to a tightening of safety standards. The crashes would have intensified scrutiny on formation flying procedures, particularly concerning spacing and sequencing between aircraft of different sizes, as well as on the competency assessments for pilots performing complex aerobatic sequences. The AAIB's investigations provided a clear blueprint for what went wrong in both cases—the vortex-induced loss of control in the Vampire and the pilot-induced spin in the Kingcobra—and these findings would have informed new guidelines and training requirements aimed at mitigating such risks in the future. The cancellation of the aircraft registration for the crashed Kingcobra by the CAA further underscores the administrative consequences of such events , .

Placing the 2001 disasters into a historical context reveals that while they were unprecedented in their timing, the venue itself was not without a history of fatal accidents. The provided sources indicate that there had been prior fatal incidents at the Biggin Hill Airshow, most notably a Douglas A-26 Invader crash on September 20, 1980, which killed the pilot and seven passengers . That tragedy prompted significant rule changes from the UK's Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), specifically prohibiting the carriage of passengers during display routines . Another fatality occurred on May 15, 1977, involving a sightseeing helicopter colliding with a de Havilland Tiger Moth biplane . The 2001 incidents, therefore, occurred nearly two decades after the last fatal accident at the venue, suggesting that despite previous regulatory improvements, new and different risks had emerged, particularly related to the complexities of modern aerobatic display routines and the physics of formation flying. The phrase "worst weekend in modern airshow history in the UK," used by a forum contributor describing the events, encapsulates the profound impact these two consecutive crashes had on the collective memory of the aviation community and the public . The cluster of fatalities in such a short period irrevocably damaged the airshow's reputation for safety and trustworthiness. The event, which annually attracted around 35,000 people, would have undergone a thorough and painful reassessment of its safety culture and risk management strategies in the years that followed , . Ultimately, the 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters serve as a somber case study in the delicate balance between spectacle and safety, a reminder that even with the best intentions and the most experienced personnel, the unforgiving nature of flight can lead to catastrophic outcomes in an instant.

The crashes would have intensified scrutiny on formation flying procedures, particularly concerning spacing and sequencing between aircraft of different sizes, as well as on the competency assessments for pilots performing complex aerobatic sequences.

The AAIB's investigations provided a clear blueprint for what went wrong in both cases—the vortex-induced loss of control in the Vampire and the pilot-induced spin in the Kingcobra—and these findings would have informed new guidelines and training requirements aimed at mitigating such risks in the future.
The cancellation of the aircraft registration for the crashed Kingcobra by the CAA further underscores the administrative consequences of such events.
Placing the 2001 disasters into a historical context reveals that while they were unprecedented in their timing, the venue itself was not without a history of fatal accidents.

The provided sources indicate that there had been prior fatal incidents at the Biggin Hill Airshow, most notably a Douglas A-26 Invader crash on September 20, 1980, which killed the pilot and seven passengers.
That tragedy prompted significant rule changes from the UK's Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), specifically prohibiting the carriage of passengers during display routines.
Another fatality occurred on May 15, 1977, involving a sightseeing helicopter colliding with a de Havilland Tiger Moth biplane.
The 2001 incidents occurred nearly two decades after the last fatal accident at the venue.
New and different risks had emerged, particularly related to the complexities of modern aerobatic display routines and the physics of formation flying, despite previous regulatory improvements.

The phrase "worst weekend in modern airshow history in the UK," used by a forum contributor describing the events, encapsulates the profound impact these two consecutive crashes had on the collective memory of the aviation community and the public.
The cluster of fatalities in such a short period irrevocably damaged the airshow's reputation for safety and trustworthiness.
The event, which annually attracted around 35,000 people, would have undergone a thorough and painful reassessment of its safety culture and risk management strategies in the years that followed.

Ultimately, the 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters serve as a somber case study in the delicate balance between spectacle and safety, a reminder that even with the best intentions and the most experienced personnel, the unforgiving nature of flight can lead to catastrophic outcomes in an instant.

Verdict on Air Show deaths
==========================

[Croydon](https://www.yourlocalguardian.co.uk/local-news/croydon-news/)

![Image 2: USA Today logo](https://www.yourlocalguardian.co.uk/resources/responsive-static/images/usa-today-logo.svg)

This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald.

A jury at Croydon Coroner's Court has reached a verdict of accidental death on two experienced pilots who died during an air display.

They heard how the men tried desperately to pull their aircraft out of a vortex which flipped them to the ground during last year's Biggin Hill Air Show.

It is believed the De-Havilland Vampire World War II craft rolled out of control after getting caught in the wingtip vortices generated by a larger plane it had been following.

Croydon Coroner's Court heard how decorated retired RAF air marshal Sir Kenneth Hayr, 66, and his safety pilot Jonathan Kerr, 33, were killed instantly when their craft ploughed into a field more than a mile away from the annual air show.

The plane had been flying with a larger craft when the formation ended in tragedy just after 6pm on June 2 last year.

Hundreds of spectators had been watching the display and as the smaller craft attempted to turn away from the Vixen it flipped upside down and crashed into a field of long grass.

Julian Hayr told the inquest his father, a decorated pilot with the RAF who was made air marshal before his retirement in 1992, had flown "every single fighter the RAF had commissioned".

And Julie Holmes described her aviation engineer brother Jonathan as a kind, caring and capable person who "lived for his passions and died living it".

Sir Kenneth Hayr, from Warwickshire, and Jonathan Kerr, from Bournemouth, died from multiple injuries.

In a poignant and touching show of unity, the families of the dead men agreed to cremate the two together and their ashes were scattered at Biggin Hill.

The inquest into the death of Guy Bancroft-Wilson, the third pilot killed in a separate accident at last year's Biggin Hill Airshow, is due to start on Thursday, May 15, at Croydon Coroner's Court. See next week's Croydon Guardian for a more in-depth report into the inquests.

Date:Sunday 3 June 2001

Type:    Bell P-63A-7BE Kingcobra

MSN: 33-37
Year of manufacture:1944

Nature:Demo/Airshow/Display
Departure airport:Biggin Hill, Kent (BQH/EGKB)
Destination airport:Biggin Hill, Kent (BQH/EGKB)
Investigating agency: AAIB

Confidence Rating: Accident investigation report completed and information captured

Narrative:The Bell P63A Kingcobra aircraft was being flown in an air display at Biggin Hill. The pilot displayed the aircraft successfully on the first day of the airshow but on the second day, at the top of a vertical manoeuvre, he appeared to lose control and the aircraft departed controlled flight before impacting the ground in a steep nose-down attitude.  The P-63 Kingcobra was being flown by Guy Bancroft-Wilson, when it crashed, sadly killing the pilot. Below is an extract from the AAIB report into the accident:   "All three aircraft waited at the holding point for Runway 03 for 15 minutes before takeoff. After take-off the aircraft held to the west of the airport for three minutes prior to commencing their display. They then ran in together and each performed a loop followed by a half cuban eight, following which, the Kingcobra broke away from the other two, as planned.   One minute later, after performing a flypast along the display line at a measured speed of 220 knots and having passed opposite the other two aircraft, the Kingcobra was seen to pull up into a rolling, climbing manoeuvre. At the top of this manoeuvre, with the aircraft partially inverted, the pilot appeared to lose control and the aircraft entered an incipient spin.   The pilot recovered the aircraft, having lost considerable height, and continued with his display. Next he flew past the crowd from left to right, carried out a wingover to the left and returned past the crowd from right to left at 190 to 195 knots. The aircraft then went out of view for some 20 seconds, in which time it was turned to the right through some 220 degrees, before running in directly towards the crowd and pulling up into the first half of a loop.  At the top of this manoeuvre, in the inverted position, full nose-up elevator was maintained and a substantial amount of right rudder was applied. The aircraft yawed to the right and then departed into an upright incipient spin. The nose dropped steeply, full nose-up elevator was maintained, and the rudder returned to neutral. The aircraft did not recover from the ensuing dive and impacted the ground in a nose down attitude at about 160 knots.   There was an immediate fire that was quickly extinguished by the attending fire crew but the pilot had suffered fatal injuries in the impact."   Damage sustained to airframe: Per the AAIB report "aircraft destroyed". As a result, the registrastion G-BTWR was cancelled by the CAA on 28-08-2002.

Narrative:The Vampire trainer was taking part in an air display along with a DH Sea Vixen. Flying behind  the other aircraft and about to follow it in a wingover manoeuvre, the Vampire Trainer was upset by jet efflux and wing tip vortices.  The Vampire Trainer rolled inverted and dived into the ground at a 45 degree angle,  banked steeply to the right. It struck the ground about 850 metres from the end of RWY 03/21 and disintegrated in flames. Only about 5 seconds elapsed between the loss of control and the ground impact. The plane was destroyed and both pilots were killed.  According to a BBC report (see link #6, second story): "The men killed in the crash have been named as Sir Ken Hayr, a former deputy chief of defence staff, from Warwickshire, and Jonathan Kerr from Bournemouth. In a statement, Mr Kerr's family said: "Jonathon was a very special person, who lived for his passion and died living it. He worked hard and achieved his ambition to reassemble and fly his own Vampire."

Registration: G-BTWR
MSN: 33-37
Year of manufacture:1944
Engine model:Allison V1710-117
Fatalities:Fatalities: 1 / Occupants: 1
Other fatalities:0

Aircraft damage: Destroyed
Category:Accident

Location:Biggin Hill, Kent (BGQ/EGKB) -
	   United Kingdom

Phase: Manoeuvring  (airshow, firefighting, ag.ops.)
Nature:Demo/Airshow/Display
Departure airport:Biggin Hill, Kent (BQH/EGKB)
Destination airport:Biggin Hill, Kent (BQH/EGKB)
Investigating agency: AAIB

Confidence Rating: Accident investigation report completed and information captured

Narrative:The Bell P63A Kingcobra aircraft was being flown in an air display at Biggin Hill. The pilot displayed the aircraft successfully on the first day of the airshow but on the second day, at the top of a vertical manoeuvre, he appeared to lose control and the aircraft departed controlled flight before impacting the ground in a steep nose-down attitude.  The P-63 Kingcobra was being flown by Guy Bancroft-Wilson, when it crashed, sadly killing the pilot. Below is an extract from the AAIB report into the accident:   "All three aircraft waited at the holding point for Runway 03 for 15 minutes before takeoff. After take-off the aircraft held to the west of the airport for three minutes prior to commencing their display. They then ran in together and each performed a loop followed by a half cuban eight, following which, the Kingcobra broke away from the other two, as planned.   One minute later, after performing a flypast along the display line at a measured speed of 220 knots and having passed opposite the other two aircraft, the Kingcobra was seen to pull up into a rolling, climbing manoeuvre. At the top of this manoeuvre, with the aircraft partially inverted, the pilot appeared to lose control and the aircraft entered an incipient spin.   The pilot recovered the aircraft, having lost considerable height, and continued with his display. Next he flew past the crowd from left to right, carried out a wingover to the left and returned past the crowd from right to left at 190 to 195 knots. The aircraft then went out of view for some 20 seconds, in which time it was turned to the right through some 220 degrees, before running in directly towards the crowd and pulling up into the first half of a loop.  At the top of this manoeuvre, in the inverted position, full nose-up elevator was maintained and a substantial amount of right rudder was applied. The aircraft yawed to the right and then departed into an upright incipient spin. The nose dropped steeply, full nose-up elevator was maintained, and the rudder returned to neutral. The aircraft did not recover from the ensuing dive and impacted the ground in a nose down attitude at about 160 knots.   There was an immediate fire that was quickly extinguished by the attending fire crew but the pilot had suffered fatal injuries in the impact."   Damage sustained to airframe: Per the AAIB report "aircraft destroyed". As a result, the registrastion G-BTWR was cancelled by the CAA on 28-08-2002.

Accident investigation:

Investigating agency: AAIB
Report number: EW/C2001/6/4
Status: Investigation completed

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article contains [dynamic lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Lists#Dynamic_lists "Wikipedia:WikiProject Lists") that may never be able to satisfy particular standards for completeness. You can help by [editing the page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century "Special:EditPage/List of air show accidents and incidents in the 20th century") to add missing items, with references to [reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources").

This is a year-by-year list of aviation accidents that have occurred at [airshows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_show "Air show") worldwide in the 20th century.

*   August 18 – [Airbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbourne_/(air_show/) "Airbourne (air show)") 2000 show ([Eastbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastbourne "Eastbourne"), East Sussex, England) – Former [Red Arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Arrows "Red Arrows") pilot Ted Girdler was killed when his [Aero L-29 Delfín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aero_L-29_Delf%C3%ADn "Aero L-29 Delfín") jet failed to pull up from a diving roll and crashed into the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-1)
*   June 18 – Willow Grove 2000 Sounds of Freedom Air Show ([Willow Grove, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow_Grove,_Pennsylvania "Willow Grove, Pennsylvania")) – Two crew members of an [F-14 Tomcat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-14_Tomcat "F-14 Tomcat") were killed when their aircraft lost altitude and crashed into a wooded area. They were demonstrating a low speed "landing wave-off maneuver" at the time of the accident.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-2)
*   March 18 – Wings Over South Texas (Kingsville NAS, Texas) – Pilot Maj. Brison Phillips was killed when his [F-16 Fighting Falcon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-16_Fighting_Falcon "F-16 Fighting Falcon") crashed at an air show while thousands of horrified spectators watched. Phillips had been attempting a [Split S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split_S "Split S") maneuver, in which the pilot rolls the airplane until it is upside down and then drops in a dive. The plane hit the ground and exploded, scattering debris for half a mile in a field about 6 miles (9.7 km) north of the naval base about 12:45 p.m.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-3)

*   October 3 – California International Airshow (Salinas, California) – Pilot [Wayne Handley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Handley "Wayne Handley") was seriously injured when his custom built Turbo Raven crashed during maneuvers. The NTSB attributed the crash to pilot error, but Handley attributed it to an engine malfunction.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]
*   September 18 – [Reno Air Races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reno_Air_Races "Reno Air Races") (also known as National Championship Air Races) Pilot Gary Levitz, 61, a 30-year race veteran of Grand Prairie, Texas, was racing his highly modified Mustang P-51, which disintegrated during the Gold Unlimited race, scattering debris and damaging a house in Lemmon Valley, just east of the Stead Airport Base, where the races were being held. The NTSB had determined that the tail [empennage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empennage "Empennage") failed in flight causing the aircraft to break apart.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]
*   September 12 – Harriman-West Airport airshow – Both pilots were killed when a [Cessna 337C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna_Skymaster "Cessna Skymaster") and a [Cessna 305C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna_O-1_Bird_Dog "Cessna O-1 Bird Dog") collided in midair while conducting in-trail fly-bys.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-4)
*   July 29 – [EAA Airventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AirVenture "AirVenture") airshow ([Oshkosh, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oshkosh,_Wisconsin "Oshkosh, Wisconsin")) – Pilot Laird Doctor was seriously injured when his [F4U Corsair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F4U_Corsair "F4U Corsair") collided with a stationary [F8F Bearcat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F8F_Bearcat "F8F Bearcat") during its takeoff roll. The Corsair crashed in flames beside the runway and was destroyed. Howard Pardue, the pilot of the Bearcat, was not seriously injured but his aircraft suffered major damage.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-5)
*   June 12 – [Paris Air Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Air_Show "Paris Air Show") (Paris, France) – A [Russian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Air_Force "Russian Air Force") [Sukhoi Su-30MKI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-30MKI "Sukhoi Su-30MKI") demonstrator '01' (with [canards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canard_/(aeronautics/) "Canard (aeronautics)") and [vectored thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_vectoring "Thrust vectoring")), crashed at [Le Bourget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Bourget "Le Bourget") Airport. At the completion of a downward spiraling maneuver, the tail contacted the grass surface. With almost no forward speed the fighter was able to pull away from the ground, wings level, with an up pitch of 10–15 degrees and climb to ~150 feet (46 m), with the right jet nozzle deflected fully up and flames engulfing the left engine. Sukhoi test pilot Vyacheslav Averynov initiated ejection with navigator Vladimir Shendrikh departing the aircraft first. The [Zvezda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPP_Zvezda "NPP Zvezda") [K-36D-3.5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-36D-3.5 "K-36D-3.5") [ejection seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejection_seat "Ejection seat") worked perfectly and both crew descended on to a taxiway unhurt. The Su-30 impacted some distance from the crew.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-6) The incident was captured on video.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-7)
*   June 6 – Milan Rastislav Stefanik airport airshow ([Bratislava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bratislava "Bratislava"), [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia")) – [Test pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_pilot "Test pilot") Graham Wardell was killed when his [BAE Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAE_Systems "BAE Systems") [Hawk 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAE_Hawk "BAE Hawk") failed to pull out of a low turn and struck the ground. A woman spectator was knocked off a nearby rooftop by the force of the explosion and died of her injuries.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-8)
*   May 30 – Airshow at [Nowra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nowra,_New_South_Wales "Nowra, New South Wales"), New South Wales, Australia. A vintage [CAC Wirraway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAC_Wirraway "CAC Wirraway") crashed during the display, killing pilot Owen O'Malley and observer Phil Lloyd.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-9)

*   August 15 – Swanton Morley Airshow ([East Dereham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Dereham "East Dereham"), Norfolk, England) – Pilot Christopher Wilkins was killed when his [Rollason D31 Turbulent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druine_Turbulent "Druine Turbulent") stalled and crashed while performing with the Tiger Club display team.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-10)
*   July 3 – During a practice flight prior to performing in the National Cherry Festival Air Show ([Traverse City, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traverse_City,_Michigan "Traverse City, Michigan")) an [Aero L-39 Albatross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aero_L-39_Albatros "Aero L-39 Albatros") went missing. Neither the plane nor its pilots were ever seen again.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-11)
*   May 19 – DARE Airshow ([Manassas, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manassas,_Virginia "Manassas, Virginia")) – Pilot Dr. Miles Merritt was killed when his [Sukhoi Su-29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-29 "Sukhoi Su-29") crashed while performing a skidding turn at too low an "[altitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_attitude "Aircraft attitude")".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-13)
*   March 1 – Mount Gambier Airshow ([Mount Gambier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Gambier,_South_Australia "Mount Gambier, South Australia"), South Australia) – An [Air Tractor AT-802](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Tractor_AT-802 "Air Tractor AT-802")A crashed on aerodrome whilst performing a low-level fire-fighting display. The pilot lost control after attempting a sudden steep climb at high speed and he was killed in the crash. There were no other casualties in the incident.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-14)

*   October 12 – ([Duxford, Cambridgeshire, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duxford "Duxford")) – The last airworthy World War II German [Messerschmitt Bf 109](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messerschmitt_Bf_109 "Messerschmitt Bf 109") crashed while being flown by Air Chief Marshal [Sir John Allison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Allison_/(RAF_officer/) "John Allison (RAF officer)"), Commander-in-Chief of [RAF Strike Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Strike_Command "RAF Strike Command"). He was unhurt despite the plane coming to rest upside down. The plane, known to be difficult to land due to poor visibility from the cockpit and its narrow-track landing gear, had overshot the runway while landing following the malfunction of its Daimler-Benz DB 605 engine.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-16)
*   September 20 – Sixth Annual Confederate Air Force Airshow ([San Marcos, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Marcos,_Texas "San Marcos, Texas")) An [Aerotek Pitts S-2A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitts_Special "Pitts Special") aerobatic biplane piloted by James Kincaid crashed at the bottom of a snap roll and dive maneuver in front of a crowd of approximately 15,000. The pilot died from his injuries later that day. Witnesses reported that the plane did not have sufficient airspeed at the start of the sequence to keep from crashing at the bottom of the dive.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-19)
*   September 14 – Chesapeake Air Show ([Middle River, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_River,_Maryland "Middle River, Maryland")) – A [Lockheed F-117](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_F-117 "Lockheed F-117"), _81–793_, of the 7th Fighter Squadron, 49th Fighter Wing, at [Holloman AFB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holloman_AFB "Holloman AFB"), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"), lost its port wing at 1500 hrs. during a pass over [Martin State Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_State_Airport "Martin State Airport"), and crashed into a residential area of [Bowley's Quarters, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowleys_Quarters,_Maryland "Bowleys Quarters, Maryland") damaging several homes. Four people on the ground received minor injuries and the pilot, Maj. Bryan "B.K." Knight, 36, escaped with minor injuries after ejecting from the aircraft.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-20) A month-long Air Force investigation found that four of 39 fasteners for the wing's structural support assembly were apparently left off when the wings were removed and reinstalled in January 1996, according to a report released on December 12, 1997.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-21)
*   July 26 – Ostend Airshow ([Ostend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostend "Ostend"), [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium")) – Captain Omar Hani Bilal of the [Jordanian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordanian_Air_Force "Jordanian Air Force") display team, the [Royal Jordanian Falcons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Jordanian_Falcons "Royal Jordanian Falcons"), was killed when he lost control of his [Walter Extra EA300s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra_300 "Extra 300"). His plane crashed at the end of the runway and burst into flames near a [Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Cross "Red Cross") tent and spectator stands. On the ground, eight were killed and forty injured.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-22)
*   June 22 – Wings Over Long Island Airshow – ([Westhampton, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westhampton,_New_York "Westhampton, New York")) – Two planes racing collided over [Francis S. Gabreski Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_S._Gabreski_Airport "Francis S. Gabreski Airport") in front of 15,000 spectators. Pilot Dick Goodlett died when his aircraft crashed and burst into flames. The second plane crash-landed, critically injuring pilot Chris Kalishek.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-23)
*   June 1 – Air Show Colorado 1997 ([Broomfield, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broomfield,_Colorado "Broomfield, Colorado")) – Ret. Colonel "Smiling Jack" Jack M. Rosamond was killed when he lost control of his restored [F-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-86 "F-86") Sabre Jet during an acrobatic loop at the [(then known as) Jefferson County Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountain_Metropolitan_Airport "Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport"). Unseasonably high temperatures combined with the natural high elevation (5,673 ft) of the airport was thought to make the air less dense than expected, leading to poor effectiveness of flight control surfaces. Nobody else was injured in the accident.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-24)

*   September 14 – Bob Heale of Spokane was killed while performing at Spokane's [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base") when his French [CAP-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAP-10 "CAP-10") crashed on its belly onto a dirt field in windy, rainy conditions at the annual Aerospace Days show. Investigators focused on possible mechanical problems with the 21-year-old plane. Bob Heale had been a regular performer at the [Silverwood Theme Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverwood_Theme_Park "Silverwood Theme Park") in Athol, Idaho.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-27)
*   August 4 – [Three Rivers Regatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Rivers_Regatta "Three Rivers Regatta") ([Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), Pennsylvania) – Pilot Clarence Speal was killed when the left hand wings on his biplane folded back which caused him to lose control and crash into the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-28)
*   July 21 – [Barton Aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barton_Aerodrome "Barton Aerodrome") air show ([Barton-upon-Irwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barton-upon-Irwell "Barton-upon-Irwell"), Greater Manchester, England) – The last [de Havilland Mosquito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Mosquito "De Havilland Mosquito") known to be airworthy (serial number RR299), a T Mk III built by D.H. at Leavesden in Spring 1945, crashed with the loss of both crew after suffering loss of engine power when performing a wing-over maneuver. The incident was captured on video.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-29)
*   July 14 – [Flying Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Legends "Flying Legends") Air Display (Duxford, Cambridgeshire, England) – Pilot Michael "Hoof" Proudfoot was killed when his [Lockheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Corporation "Lockheed Corporation") [P-38 Lightning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-38_Lightning "P-38 Lightning") aircraft crashed and cartwheeled while performing a roll maneuver. Several aircraft on the ground were damaged or destroyed.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-30)
*   June 2 – Bartlesville Biplane Exposition ([Bartlesville, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartlesville,_Oklahoma "Bartlesville, Oklahoma")) – Two Biplanes clipped wings on landing, all four aboard killed: William Watson, 71; John Halterman, 51; Rodney Bogan, 41; and Annette Delahay, 45.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-31)
*   4 May – Sertoma Cajun Air Festival ([Lafayette, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lafayette,_Louisiana "Lafayette, Louisiana")) – Pilot Joe Hartung, 44, perished when the Canadian-built Harvard Mk. II he was flying hit the runway while performing a low altitude roll.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-33)
*   April 27 – Shiloh Airshow ([Stoneville, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoneville,_North_Carolina "Stoneville, North Carolina")) – Pilot Lindsey Hess escaped injury when his [Pitts S2 A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitts_Special "Pitts Special") crashed inverted on the runway following his attempt to cut a ribbon with the plane.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-34)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-35)
*   April 16 – [EAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_Aircraft_Association "Experimental Aircraft Association") [Sun 'n Fun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_%27n_Fun "Sun 'n Fun") ([Lakeland, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakeland,_Florida "Lakeland, Florida")) – Pilot [Charlie Hillard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Hillard "Charlie Hillard") was killed when his [Hawker Sea Fury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Sea_Fury "Hawker Sea Fury") flipped over while landing in a crosswind.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-STPETE1-36)

*   September 9 – ([Johannisthal, Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannisthal_Air_Field "Johannisthal Air Field")) – A [DASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DaimlerChrysler_Aerospace "DaimlerChrysler Aerospace")\-operated [Messerschmitt Bf 108](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messerschmitt_Bf_108 "Messerschmitt Bf 108") Taifun, _D-EFPT_,[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-37) crashed during an airshow, killing pilot Gerd Kahdemann and passenger [Reinhard Furrer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhard_Furrer "Reinhard Furrer"), a former astronaut who had flown in space for Germany in 1985 during the [STS-61A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61A "STS-61A") mission aboard the [Space Shuttle _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger").[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-38) After completing an aerobatic display, the Bf 108 was seen to climb and attempt an aileron turn with increased pitch which developed into a barrel-roll into the ground at a ~90-degree angle. A piece of the airframe that came loose while the aircraft was inverted was found to be the starboard wing leading edge slat.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-39)
*   September 2 – [Canadian International Air Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_International_Air_Show "Canadian International Air Show") (Toronto, Ontario) – Seven [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") crew members were killed when their [Hawker Siddeley Nimrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Siddeley_Nimrod "Hawker Siddeley Nimrod") MR.2P stalled during a low altitude turn and crashed into [Lake Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Ontario "Lake Ontario").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-40)

Lars Rådeström, the same pilot as in the 1989 incident [ejected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejection_seat "Ejection seat") safely. Despite large crowds standing by watching, no one on the ground was seriously injured. *   July 24 – [Lebanon, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon,_New_Hampshire "Lebanon, New Hampshire") – A biplane collided with a parachutist in the opening act of the Lebanon Airshow. No one on the ground was injured.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-53) The incident was captured on video.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-54)

Poage died after crashing his red-and-white [Pitts S-2B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitts_Special "Pitts Special") during an air show at [Martin State Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_State_Airport "Martin State Airport") after he added a fourth corkscrew maneuver to three that were expected during a nosedive. Tope was killed when his [P-51 Mustang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-51_Mustang "P-51 Mustang") crashed into a golf course.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-71)

*   August 28 – Kleine Brogel Air Base ([Peer, Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer,_Belgium "Peer, Belgium")) Pilot Ari Piippo was killed when the [Aermacchi M-290 RediGO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aermacchi_M-290_RediGO "Aermacchi M-290 RediGO") he was demonstrating failed to come out of a spin.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-:0-81)

Giorgio Alessio were killed, wreckage from the collision landed on the spectators, killing 31 people outright, mortally wounding 39 more and seriously injuring 346. [Until 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sknyliv_air_show_disaster "Sknyliv air show disaster"), this was the deadliest airshow accident.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]
*   August 7 – [Leopoldsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldsburg "Leopoldsburg"), Belgium – Belgian Air Force pilot Michel Duvivier was killed when his [Mirage 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_5 "Dassault Mirage 5") jet crashed at an air show organized by the Belgian Air Force.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-:0-81)

Cadick was subjected to extremely high G forces that resulted in his face making contact with the control stick, sustaining serious injuries. *   August 8 – Fairfield County Air Show, [Lancaster, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster,_Ohio "Lancaster, Ohio") – Pilot James King was killed when his biplane crashed while performing at the air show.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-87)

*   June 28 – SHAPE International Air Show, Chièvres Air Base, Belgium – After hovering a Hawker Siddeley Harrier GR.3 with a rearward movement, parallel to the public line at about 200 meters of altitude, R.A.F. Flt. Lt. Brian D. Weatherley ended with a nose down attitude that seemed steeper than usual. The aircraft nose kept going down past a recoverable angle. The pilot ejected while the aircraft was pointing straight towards the ground, still roughly stationary. He hit the ground before his parachute opened and later died from injuries sustained in the ejection. After the pilot ejected, the airplane went almost belly up and fell to the ground with a loud boom, explosion and black smoke.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-88)
*   July 24 – RAF Brawdy Air Show, Wales UK. A US Phantom jet crashed into the sea off the coast. There were no injuries on the ground.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-89)
*   26 May – Berlin Municipal Airport (Milan, New Hampshire) – Pilot Robert Weymouth, known as "The Flying Farmer", was killed when he failed to recover during a descent.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-90)
*   26 May – Mildenhall Air Show ([Mildenhall, Suffolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mildenhall,_Suffolk "Mildenhall, Suffolk")) – The crew of a RAF Meteor was killed following the mid air collision with a RAF [Vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Vampire "De Havilland Vampire"). The crew of the Vampire was able to parachute to safety.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-91)

*   July 13 – Western New York Air Show '85 ([Niagara Falls International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls_International_Airport "Niagara Falls International Airport"), New York) – [Blue Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Angels "Blue Angels") Aircraft 5, BuNo _155029_, and 6, BuNo _154992_, both [Douglas A-4F Skyhawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_A-4_Skyhawk "Douglas A-4 Skyhawk"), collided at the top of a loop, killing Lt. Cmdr. Michael Gershon. The other pilot, Lt. Andy Caputi, ejected safely with only minor injuries. *   April 27 – An [AT-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_T-6_Texan "North American T-6 Texan") crashed during an air show at the [El Toro Marine Corps Air Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Toro_Marine_Corps_Air_Station "El Toro Marine Corps Air Station") when it apparently lost power, snagged a power line, smacked into the street and then slid into the chapel, killing the pilot Merrel Richard Gossman, 55, and passenger Robert G. *   September 4 – A de Havilland Canada DHC-5D Buffalo plane, registered C-GCTC, was damaged beyond repair in an accident during the 1984 Farnborough Airshow. The aircraft then landed very hard. The nose gear collapsed, both wings failed and the propellers disintegrated after contacting the runway. Debris caused some damage to vehicles and three aircraft in the static display area.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-98)

*   June 3 – Großostheim near Aschaffenburg, Germany – A Hawker Siddeley Harrier GR3 launched vertically for a demonstration flight in front of the audience. From a height of about 90feet the Harrier crashed next to the runway and burst into flames – around 100 feet away from the audience. The pilot was able to escape with the ejection seat but the falling seat killed a spectator.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-101)

All 46 aboard were killed. The crash was later found to be caused by an accumulation of ground [walnut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walnut "Walnut") shells that had been used to clean the machinery.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-111)[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-112)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-113)
*   16 May – Shelby County Air Show ([Alabaster, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabaster,_Alabama "Alabaster, Alabama")) Pilot Don Smith was killed when his [Piper J-3 Cub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piper_J-3_Cub "Piper J-3 Cub") failed to pull out of a spin.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-114)
*   January 18 – ([Indian Springs Air Force Auxiliary Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Springs_Air_Force_Auxiliary_Field "Indian Springs Air Force Auxiliary Field")) – All 4 USAF Thunderbirds pilots were killed in the [Diamond crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Thunderbirds_Indian_Springs_Diamond_Crash "1982 Thunderbirds Indian Springs Diamond Crash").[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-115)

Hauk, in Thunderbird 6, crashed while attempting to land his ailing T-38 after an engine malfunctioned and caught fire. With black smoke billowing from the exhaust and the aircraft losing altitude in a high nose-up attitude, the safety officer on the ground radioed Capt Hauck: "You’re on fire, punch out", to which he responded: “Hang on... we have a bunch of people down there”. The aircraft continued to fight to stay airborne for about half a mile before hitting a large oak tree and a barn, then sliding across a field and flipping as it traversed an irrigation canal ultimately erupting into a fireball just a few hundred feet from the runway's end. No one on the ground was injured even though the accident occurred adjacent to a roadway packed with onlookers.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-117)

*   September 21 – Joliet Park District Airport ([Joliet, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joliet,_Illinois "Joliet, Illinois")) – Three United States Marine service members were killed and one injured when their [Huey H-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_UH-1_Iroquois "Bell UH-1 Iroquois") helicopter stalled and crashed when it pulled up from a low high speed pass.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-118)
*   September 21 – ([Biggin Hill, London, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport "London Biggin Hill Airport")) – A [Douglas A-26 Invader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_A-26_Invader "Douglas A-26 Invader") [crashed during an air display](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Biggin_Hill_Invader_crash "1980 Biggin Hill Invader crash"). The pilot and seven passengers were killed. The [Civil Aviation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Aviation_Authority_of_the_United_Kingdom "Civil Aviation Authority of the United Kingdom") subsequently introduced rules preventing passengers from being carried during air displays.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-119)
*   June 15 – (Shannon Airport, [Fredericksburg, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredericksburg,_Virginia "Fredericksburg, Virginia")) – Sgt. 1st Class Tom Johnson, a parachute jumper with the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army "U.S. Army") [Golden Knights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Parachute_Team "United States Army Parachute Team"), fell over 10,000 feet to his death when both of his parachutes (main and reserve) failed to deploy.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-120)
*   April 17 – American Samoan Flag Day ([Pago Pago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pago_Pago "Pago Pago"), American Samoa) – The seven member crew of an American Navy [P-3 Orion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_P-3_Orion "Lockheed P-3 Orion") were killed when their plane struck a cable car wire, lost its right wing and tail, and cartwheeled into a local hotel causing a fire. Navy Lieutenant Michael Curtin was killed.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-126) The accident was caught on film.

Aircraft written off.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]
*   September 23 – Suffolk Air Fair press preview ([Westhampton Beach, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westhampton_Beach,_New_York "Westhampton Beach, New York")) – Stunt pilot Edward H. *   August 21 – Evergreen Airpark – Vancouver Washington. Stunt pilot Harry Eyerly was killed when his Pitts Special failed to recover from a spin.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-132)
*   June 3 – Paris Air Show (Paris, France) – Test pilot Howard W. Dewenter was credited with saving many lives by landing at the [Buffalo Niagara International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Niagara_International_Airport "Buffalo Niagara International Airport") despite the runway deemed too short to stop. Flying a [Grumman F-11 Tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grumman_F-11_Tiger "Grumman F-11 Tiger") he was able to bring the plane down and stop without injury to others.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]
*   September 20 – Prototype [Avro Vulcan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avro_Vulcan "Avro Vulcan") _VX770_ in an airshow at [RAF Syerston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Syerston "RAF Syerston") suffers total collapse of the plane's right wing. The plane, the first aircraft built in a newly independent Poland, was a copy of a [Hannover CL.II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannover_CL.II "Hannover CL.II") and crashed due to faulty cabling.[\[352\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-352)
*   August 15 – [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), Maryland – While performing aerial stunts at [Patterson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patterson_Park "Patterson Park") a military aircraft crash landed through a fence and into a baseball diamond killing three children and injuring a number of others.[\[353\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-353)
*   July 17 – [Americus, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americus,_Georgia "Americus, Georgia") – Sergeant Gordon Gates, of the Army Air Services, was killed when his safety belt failed while he was flying inverted during an air circus. His plane continued flying unmanned for a half a mile before finally crashing.[\[354\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-354)

*   June 25 – **Charles Franklin Niles** was an early aviator having been taught by [Glenn Curtiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Curtiss "Glenn Curtiss") in 1913.[\[355\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-355) It was stated in his obituary that he was the first to fly around the [Statue of Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty "Statue of Liberty"), and that he served as an aviator in the 1910–1920 [Mexican Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Revolution "Mexican Revolution").[\[356\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-356) On June 25, 1916, while flying a loop maneuver in his [Moisant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moisant_Aviation_School "Moisant Aviation School") monoplane at the [Oshkosh, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oshkosh,_Wisconsin "Oshkosh, Wisconsin") fairgrounds a wing collapsed and he crashed. He died of his injuries the next day.[\[357\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-357) A witness to the crash was cartoonist [Robert Osborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Osborn_/(satirist/) "Robert Osborn (satirist)").[\[358\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-358)

*   October 25 – Panama–Pacific International Exposition (San Francisco, California) – Pilot Charles Niles was injured when he crashed while landing during an exhibition flight.[\[359\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-359)
*   September 22 – Colorado State Fair (Pueblo, Colorado) – Parachutist Eddie Coy was killed when his parachute malfunctioned after he jumped from a balloon at a height of 1,800 feet.[\[360\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-360)
*   March 14 – San Francisco, California – Famed aerialist [Lincoln Beachey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Beachey "Lincoln Beachey"), performing at the [Panama–Pacific International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama%E2%80%93Pacific_International_Exposition "Panama–Pacific International Exposition") before a crowd of at least 50,000 onlookers, attempted the first exhibition of inverted flight in a monoplane. Beginning the stunt only 2000 feet above the waters of [San Francisco Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay "San Francisco Bay"), Beachey pulled sharply on the controls to resume level flight, but the resulting pressure on the wing spars caused them to snap and the plane plunged into the water. Beachey actually survived the crash but drowned as rescuers were unable to extract him for nearly two hours.[\[361\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-361)

*   April 19 – Buc, Normandy France: Two monoplanes collided resulting in two seriously injured and two killed. André Bidot and his passenger Mr. Pellato, collides with the aeroplane flown by François Deroye and passenger Mr. Dablin at around 16:30. A third aircraft taking part in the chase, piloted by a Mr. Coendett, was not involved in the collision and landed safely. Deroye's aircraft caught fire and both he and Mr. Dablin perished in the flames. Bidot's aircraft crashed relatively intact, but caught fire after impact, seriously injuring Bidot and Mr. Pellato.[\[362\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-362)

*   October 7 – [Hammondsport, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammondsport,_New_York "Hammondsport, New York") – One spectator was killed and several injured when they were knocked off a roof by the wing of an aircraft piloted by [Lincoln J. Beachey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_J._Beachey "Lincoln J. Beachey"). He escaped injury when he crashed following the accident.[\[364\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-364)
*   October 1 – Randolph County Fairgrounds ([Elkins, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elkins,_West_Virginia "Elkins, West Virginia")) – Pilot Irving Conley along with several spectators were injured when his aircraft fell from a height of fifty feet.[\[365\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-365)
*   October 1 – Binghamton Industrial Exposition (Binghamton, New York) – Pilot Earl V. Fritts escaped injury when he glided his aircraft to earth following the failure of his propeller and crankshaft while flying at an altitude of 500 feet.[\[366\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-366)
*   September 25 – Mesa County Fair (Grand Junction, Colorado) – Pilot H.W. Blakely suffered minor injuries when his aircraft crashed following an engine stall while he was flying at a height of 85 feet.[\[367\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-367)
*   September 9 – [Carmi, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmi,_Illinois "Carmi, Illinois") – Pilot Tony Jannus escaped injury when he landed his aircraft after the carburetor fell off his engine while flying at an altitude of 900 feet during an exhibition flight.[\[368\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-368)
*   August 6 – Carnival Week (Victoria, British Columbia, Canada) – Pilot Johnny Bryant was killed when his aircraft crashed during an exhibition flight at the water carnival celebrations.[\[369\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-369)
*   July 19 – [Golden Potlatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Potlatch "Golden Potlatch") (Seattle, Washington) – Parachutist Francis L. Thayer was killed when his parachute harness broke at a height of 600 feet and he fell into Puget Sound.[\[370\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_air_show_accidents_and_incidents_in_the_20th_century#cite_note-370)
